summary.title: Features of your font you had no idea about
summary.one_liner: You learn how OpenType features and variable font axes (wght, wdth, slnt, opsz, custom axes) can be used from CSS, including stylistic alternates, swashes, numerals, small caps and contextual alternates.
keywords: how to use font features in css
takeaways: Variable font axes like wght, wdth, slnt and opsz can be set with CSS properties such as font-weight, or with font-variation-settings for other axes.
font-variation-settings and font-variant-alternates do not cascade well; defining them on a child overwrites the parent's values, so CSS variables are a workaround.
Stylistic alternates come in three forms: salt for all letters, stylistic sets (ss01 etc.), and single character variants (cv01 etc.).
Numerals can be lining or old-style and tabular or proportional, selected with font-variant-numeric; small caps use font-variant-caps.
Contextual alternates are on by default and can be disabled with font-variant-ligatures.
summary.summary: The article is a web typography guide that explains the extra features packed into high-quality OpenType fonts beyond basic weights and italics. It walks through variable font axes and how to control them from CSS, then covers alternates (salt, stylistic sets, character variants), swashes, numeral styles, small caps, and contextual alternates, with code examples for each. It closes with pointers to further reading on OpenType and variable fonts.
